title: Top 15, Starbucks: This Time, the New Store Is in Luoyang
excerpt: "This is a Starbucks store first, and a Luoyang store second." Starbucks now has more than 1,600 stores in China, and most of its new ones are in second- and third-tier cities.
body:
"This is a Starbucks store first, and a Luoyang store second." Starbucks now has more than 1,600 stores in China, and most of its new ones are in second- and third-tier cities.

"No. 1."

At 7:56 a.m. on May 15, Liu Songhao, who likes a Vanilla Frappuccino in summer, posted those two words on WeChat Moments, with a photo of the "Starbucks Coffee" logo.

"I just wanted to be the first customer at Starbucks in Luoyang," Liu said.

So he arrived at the Wangfujing department store location at 7:40. Three hours later he walked in between two lines of a dozen or so Starbucks staff and reporters, and got his wish.

The next day a photo of him holding the Luoyang city mug ran in *Dahe Daily*, the biggest newspaper in Henan Province, and he posted again: "Many thanks to XX for setting me on the road to Starbucks show-off."

Luoyang's first Starbucks customer could only be one person, but many more were waiting outside for the opening.

Before the doors opened, about 40 customers, men and women, young and old, stood outside. An hour before the store opened to the public, an opening ceremony for officials, the media and customer representatives was under way inside, so they peered in through the glass walls. Inside, some guests sipped drinks Starbucks had laid on, some listened to the host talk about coffee, and some took selfies.

At 11 o'clock sharp, the Wangfujing store opened. The first wave of customers were mostly regulars: in every group of two or three, one had a Starbucks Rewards card, knew the names of the cup sizes and knew exactly what to order.

By 11:35 the first rush had passed. Most people took their drinks to go, and the store grew quiet again.

![Customers at the opening of the Starbucks store in Luoyang](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160607122732zG3OnV1cZtwsWNlj.jpg-w600)

Four years after opening its first store in Zhengzhou, Starbucks has made Luoyang its second city in Henan. It already has 13 stores in Zhengzhou.

Luoyang is one of the most important ancient cities in Chinese history. The word "China" (*zhongguo*) first appears in the inscription "*zhai zi zhongguo*" ("dwell in this central land"), cast on the He Zun, a bronze vessel from the early Western Zhou, and it refers to the Heluo region centered on Luoyang. In the Eastern Han, Luoyang replaced Chang'an as the starting point of the Silk Road, and today it is still counted among the "ancient capitals of six dynasties."

In his poem "Passing the Old City of Luoyang," the Northern Song statesman Sima Guang left a somewhat sweeping footnote: "If you would know the rise and fall of all the ages, look only at the city of Luoyang." Whatever one makes of that, the history this modern city inherited has been turned into tourism. The White Horse Temple, the first temple built after Buddhism reached China, the Longmen Grottoes, and the peony fair held every April and May all keep Luoyang from vanishing among cities of its size.

With more than 6.55 million people, Luoyang also scores well commercially. In *CBN Weekly*'s "New First-Tier" city survey, Luoyang ranks 43rd among Chinese cities and is classed as a "second-tier city." Starbucks told QDaily that one of its main tests for entering a city is whether a fairly mature coffee-drinking culture already exists. Luoyang already has 238 cafes and 147 Western restaurants.

![Luoyang's coffee and dining landscape](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/201606071227337wBzOoYDjqAhI92G.jpg-w600)

Last October, when Starbucks posted job ads for its Luoyang stores on its website, a report surfaced online that it would open a store in the Longmen Grottoes scenic area. In the end, though, Starbucks put its first two Luoyang stores in two big shopping centers on either bank of the Luo River: Quanshun Shopping Center and Wangfujing Shopping Center.

"Starbucks mainly targets business people, so a CBD is the ideal location. But in a place like Luoyang, which has no clear CBD, it will choose large malls, or sites near government offices, where it can get steady foot traffic and customers with some spending power," said Tang Wenhua, deputy managing director for North China at JLL.

Directly north of Quanshun Shopping Center stands the new Luoyang municipal government building. Between the two lies a local landmark, a musical fountain that claims to have once been the largest in Asia, which draws a crowd every Tuesday, Thursday and Saturday evening. And of Luoyang's four authorized Apple resellers, the one in Quanshun Plaza is so far the only one selling the Apple Watch, which says something about the mall's standing among the city's shopping malls.

Starbucks has a plaza storefront here, separate from the main building, with 230 square meters indoors and a 160-square-meter outdoor area. "Before we moved in, this space had always been empty," said Ren Longfei, manager of the Quanshun store. He takes that as a vote of confidence in Starbucks from the landlord.

![Starbucks at Quanshun Shopping Center](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160607122734pK63zuUHRY8l0GTt.jpg-w600)

Starbucks at Quanshun Shopping Center

The other store is in Wangfujing Shopping Center, which opened only on May 9 and is Luoyang's second Wangfujing. Unlike the Quanshun store, it sits in Jianxi District, once crowded with factories. On a 100-meter lane near the mall there are 10 different local noodle shops, which gives a rough idea of how residential the area is.

The new mall bills itself as the new landmark for Luoyang's young people, and its opening slogan reads: "For Luoyang's latest trends, look here." In a list compiled by the Weibo account @LuochengGonglue, Wangfujing Shopping Center was called, bluntly, "where only the fair, rich and beautiful shop." At the ground-floor entrance it has squeezed in a sculpture exhibition, and in the basement, home to an imported-goods supermarket and assorted food stalls, it has posted a few alpacas and miniature pigs to draw crowds. Besides Starbucks, the mall has brought in Pizza Hut, Pacific Coffee and Zoo Coffee, brands still fairly rare in the city.

None of them carries the weight of Starbucks, though: only Starbucks made it onto the mobile billboards outside the mall. At the opening, Wangfujing and Starbucks were each using the other to draw attention.

High-quality coffee, a comfortable place to sit, professional service and a varied coffee culture: these are what Starbucks publicly says it pursues. Euromonitor's analysis credits the same things with helping it build brand recognition and win customers in second- and third-tier cities.

There is another factor. Zhengzhou, the provincial capital an hour from Luoyang by train, Wuhan to the south and Xi'an to the west each already have at least 10 Starbucks stores, and people traveling among these cities have spread the word.

Xiao Hu, who works in a government office, went in for a drink on the second day of the Wangfujing store's trial run and happened to find a high school classmate working a shift there. It was not his first taste of Starbucks, though, Luoyang native as he is. Back in 2008 he had his first Starbucks coffee in Wuhan, where he went to university.

"Back then the first Starbucks opened at Qunguang Plaza in Wuhan, and the crowd was even crazier than at the Luoyang opening," Xiao Hu recalled. Years later, he clearly knows Starbucks well. He has a Starbucks Rewards card and has settled on his own ordering rules: "In summer it's always a half-sugar Matcha Frappuccino, in winter it's a Vanilla Latte without fail. Nothing else suits me."

"It's finally come to Luoyang, ha ha." That, Xiao Hu said, was his first reaction on seeing the Luoyang store. He was happy.

![Starbucks at Wangfujing Shopping Center](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160607122734bfaHVjzxr0EmJQ9Y.jpg-w600)

Starbucks at Wangfujing Shopping Center

Still, Xiao Hu, who earns about 6,000 yuan a month, admits Starbucks is not cheap for people at his level. Luoyang, whose license plates begin with "Yu C," is generally regarded as Henan's second city. Yet according to the Henan Provincial Bureau of Statistics, per capita disposable income of Luoyang's urban residents in the first three quarters of 2014 was 20,008 yuan. That is second in the province only to Zhengzhou's 21,410 yuan, but still fairly low by national standards.

"But Starbucks has no need to worry about its market. The lines every day are the best proof," Xiao Hu said.

Starbucks formally entered China in 1999. For the next 10 years it opened 30-50 stores a year. From 2012 the pace picked up sharply: 204 new stores in 2012, 317 in 2013, and in 2014 almost one a day. Now with 1,600 stores in China, Starbucks is reaching more and more second- and third-tier cities. According to Euromonitor, its share of China's coffee market rose from 12.6% in 2009 to 37% in 2014.

![Chart: Starbucks store openings in China over the years](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/201606071227352TzscZMgyA3dlvHR.jpg-w600)

After the smooth Luoyang opening, stores in Yueyang, Hunan, and Mianyang, Sichuan, have opened or will open on May 22 and May 29. Inside Starbucks, this run is called "Three Yangs Bring Good Fortune," after the auspicious saying *san yang kai tai*.

According to IOC data, per capita coffee consumption in China has grown 30% a year since 1998, and the number of coffee shops in large and medium-sized cities has grown steadily at 25% a year.

No one doubts the size of the Chinese market, and for coffee, a drink almost wholly imported, the potential looks bigger still. But it is a complicated market. Ahead of Starbucks are look-alike rivals such as Costa Coffee and Pacific Coffee; behind it are Zoo Coffee and Caffe Bene, which have sprung up in recent years, along with a string of rising local specialty coffee brands.

Apart from its late closing hours, which have added to Luoyang's nightlife, and its fashionable brand, the thing I heard most often in random interviews, the strongest impression many locals have of Starbucks, was "standard and orderly." In their eyes, beyond the brand itself, standardized operations and store design give Starbucks a more concrete guarantee of a smooth start.

"We finished hiring all the baristas six months ago. Their backgrounds vary, but almost none of them had ever made coffee. Then we sent them to Starbucks stores across Zhengzhou and trained them for about five months," Ren Longfei, the Quanshun store manager, told me.

This is Starbucks' standard training process, and Ren went through it himself. In 2011, as one of the first employees hired for Starbucks' Zhengzhou opening, he was sent to the Qunguang Plaza store in Wuhan for training. This time, as a Black Apron barista, he was transferred from Zhengzhou to Luoyang as store manager, and he has been running the store for eight months.

Besides staff training, Starbucks has an internal "Coffee Partner Homecoming Program." Zhang Jianbo and You Sheng, Luoyang natives who had worked at the Beijing airport store, were able to rejoin Starbucks when the Luoyang stores opened. "My bartending job in Luoyang actually paid more than this, but when I saw Starbucks open here I still wanted to come back," You Sheng said. Starbucks, for its part, welcomes experienced staff like them.

Sending baristas to a more mature market first is partly an advantage only a company with Starbucks' reach can use. It also shows the company's caution and patience. On the product side, that caution means it did not bring its seasonal drinks to Luoyang.

"We want to push the most classic drinks first," Ren said. By classics he means the basics: latte, cappuccino, caramel macchiato, Americano, mocha and Frappuccino. You can see the intent in both the merchandise wall and the bar displays.

"For one thing, customers accept them easily; for another, it makes it easier for us to get our message across. Say we push lattes now and people try them. Then when we bring in the French Vanilla Latte next year, it will come as a pleasant surprise," Ren added.

This is in fact Starbucks' brand strategy: in mature first-tier cities, draw customers with a stream of new products; in second- and third-tier cities, the priority for now is opening stores.

Besides operating rules, the other way Starbucks expresses standardization is design.

Four years ago, Starbucks began building a design team in China, which now has 47 people. Apart from stores in South China, which a 20-person team at its Seattle headquarters designs, the great majority of new stores are now the work of these local designers.

Li Jianhua is one of them. An interior designer with 10 years' experience, he designed the Wangfujing store on his own. Along the way, besides drawing on his own expertise, he talked things through with colleagues in development and operations who handle the practical side. Two months later he handed the drawings to colleagues in the construction department and went off to work out the specific decorations with outside suppliers.

His concept for the Wangfujing store was a friendly third place with a local Luoyang flavor, suited to residents' daily lives. Starbucks has a design guideline for every store, but much of the finer detail is left to the designer.

"We don't want to drag so-called symbolic things into the store in a heavy-handed way," Li said. So for the largest decorative painting in the store, he used a wall-sized printed coffee flower as a tribute to the peony, Luoyang's city flower. He also went out of his way to collect folk objects from the Central Plains, such as hand baskets, clay jars, small folding stools and drums, to make the store feel more down-to-earth.

![Interior of the Wangfujing Starbucks store in Luoyang](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160607122735AkILaRVs0lnmBvKY.jpg-w600)

"Luoyang is an ancient city with real character and deep cultural roots. So we have to get the culture right first, and only then think about the business," Li said.

He also used plenty of standard Starbucks elements. In line with Starbucks' environmental principles, he used reclaimed pine on the walls and built the store's huge communal table from walnut, and kept a fixed share of simple design on the columns and ceiling. On the walls he hung a large old photo of Starbucks' first store, at Pike Place Market, an artwork explaining how coffee beans are processed, and a set of photos showing the whole journey from coffee cherry to cup.

"This is a Starbucks store first, and a Luoyang store second," Li said.
